analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to document job and wage impacts and weigh alternatives before issuing regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a single cosponsor, committee vote, or floor vote over the life of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal rulemaking process. Agencies would have to base every factual finding on evidence, formally consider alternatives including taking no action at all, and weigh costs and benefits — including estimated effects on jobs, wages, economic growth, and low-income populations. Any rule projected to cut employment or average weekly wages in a specific industry by 1% or more would be labeled a "negative-impact on jobs and wages rule," creating a defined category that regulated parties could use to challenge rules in court [S3] [S2]. In practice, this would make federal rules — on workplace safety, pollution, consumer protection, and finance — slower to issue and easier to litigate away. It never advanced past referral to a House committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing potential new federal regulations. The bill would give them added procedural grounds to slow, weaken, or overturn rules they dislike, and would let any rule projected to reduce jobs or wages in their sector by 1% or more be flagged and contested [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies to consider the legal authority for a rule, the significance of the problem, existing rules, and a range of alternatives — including no federal response — before issuing a rule [S3].

Requires formal cost-benefit analysis of alternatives, including estimated net job gains or losses, wage impacts, effects on economic growth and competitiveness, and impacts on low-income populations [S3].

Defines a "negative-impact on jobs and wages rule" as any rule projected to reduce employment or average weekly wages in a NAICS-coded sector by 1% or more annually, or to reduce employment in any industry area with unemployment above 5%, creating a category vulnerable industries could invoke in court [S3].
The bill's stated purpose includes clarifying judicial review of agency interpretations and ensuring analysis of impacts on small entities, both of which expand opportunities to challenge rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on federal regulations — workers counting on safety rules, communities affected by pollution, consumers protected from unsafe products and predatory finance. Rules would take longer to finalize and face new court challenges, delaying or diluting protections [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: People who rely on federal regulations

drawbacks.text: The bill would function as a procedural chokepoint on regulation: adding mandatory analysis of alternatives, formal cost-benefit findings, and a new job-and-wage trigger would slow or block protective rules on workplace safety, environment, and consumer protection, and create openings for endless litigation by regulated parties [S3].

The job and wage triggers rest on uncertain economic projections — a 1% employment decline in a narrow 6-digit industry code is hard to forecast reliably — so the designation could be driven by modeling choices rather than real effects, cutting both ways for supporters and opponents [S3].
An honest supporter would concede the added analytical and documentation burdens carry real costs: slower rulemaking, more staff time, and delays even for rules with strong public benefits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is procedural accountability — forcing agencies to prove their rules are justified and consider less intrusive options. But the same machinery serves as a delay-and-litigation lever for regulated industries, and the job-loss trigger would apply to nearly any rule a regulated sector claims will cost jobs, regardless of whether the projection holds. The transparency benefits are modest; the risk to the timeliness and durability of public protections is substantial. Given that it drew zero cosponsors from either party, few in Congress found the trade worth making.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the bill on May 17, 2021, with no cosponsors joining at any point [S1] [S4] [S5].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and on November 9, 2021 was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly from the bill's death, but the people who rely on federal protections — workers, consumers, and communities affected by pollution — are no worse off than before. Regulated industries gained nothing they could not have pursued through other channels. The outcome mostly reflects a bill that attracted no support from either party.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal regulatory protections

for.name: Rep. Tim Burchett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never reported the bill out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no party split can be measured.

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (manufacturers, energy, mining, finance)
industries.note: The bill would give regulated businesses new procedural and litigation grounds to delay, weaken, or overturn federal rules — including a defined trigger for any rule projected to cost jobs or wages in their sector. Their gain would come directly at the cost of slower, weaker public protections.

The bill's stated purpose includes ensuring complete analysis of rules' impacts on small entities, which would give small firms more leverage against new compliance requirements — through the same mechanism that weakens protections for their customers and workers.

Expanded documentation requirements and clarified judicial review of agency interpretations would create more challenges to agency rules, generating work for lawyers who represent regulated parties challenging regulations.
